blocks.html: A desktop platform that lets finance teams issue and govern corporate cards while giving employees a fast, low-friction way to get reimbursed.

As lead designer on this project, I owned the design end to end, from early wireframes to final flows, and stayed involved through implementation and as new requirements came in. The product launched in beta while we were still collecting performance data.

blocks.title: Metrics being tracked in beta:
items: Card usage vs. receipt upload compliance
Less spending happening outside the approved process

items.challenge: Limited oversight across teams until it's too late to act

items.goal: Approve expenses without it slowing down their day
items.challenge: Everything is manual and disconnected from actual spending

items.goal: Submit an expense and move on
items.challenge: Uploading receipts and tracking reimbursements takes too much effort

blocks.html: Employees wanted things to move fast and feel simple. Finance wanted to know exactly where the money was going. Lean too far toward speed and you lose control of spend; lean too far toward control and people go back to spreadsheets and email just to get things done.
These came from informal user interviews, plus a look at how Spendesk, Pleo, and Captio handle similar tradeoffs.

items.finding: Users wanted control when OCR made mistakes.
items.insight: Make every extracted field editable, with manual entry always available.

items.finding: Finance needed spending control before cards were used.
items.insight: Add manager-set card limits and usage restrictions before issuing the card.

items.finding: One-off purchases were happening outside approval flows.
items.insight: Combine procurement requests and virtual card creation into a single approved flow.

blocks.html: In each case, the goal was the same: let people move quickly, but keep finance able to step in if something looks off.

Since the platform is in beta, results are early signals rather than confirmed outcomes:

items.html: Stakeholders validated the reimbursement and card flows pre-development, reducing rework during build
Informal testing showed employees better understood expense-to-report linking once status logic (draft, ready, submitted) was made explicit
Manager feedback prompted the addition of bulk expense actions, now in the roadmap
The team is watching reimbursement turnaround time and receipt-upload compliance as the first real indicators of whether the design reduces friction without weakening control

blocks.html: The hardest part wasn't designing for any single user — it was designing the seams between roles, where one person's convenience becomes another's risk. What surprised me most was how much trust came from giving users an escape hatch (manual entry, editable OCR) rather than trying to make automation perfect. Next, the focus shifts to validating these early signals against real usage data and tightening the procurement-to-card handoff based on manager feedback.
